reasoning: Palestinian bukra, with byiTla3 for 'it rises' and iS-Sub7 with the il- assimilating to ص. The idiom means 'tomorrow the day will dawn', i.e. things will get better. The exact wording is fairly fixed but the vowelling of the verb varies a little.
Literally 'I'll see you', with the b- present or future prefix and -ak for a male addressee. A very common Palestinian parting phrase.

Shadda doubles the emphatic ظ, written TH TH per the scheme. Taa marbuta after ف is e. The word is of MSA origin but normal in everyday Palestinian speech. The exact realisation of ظ (emphatic z or D) is the uncertain part.
Past tense, he-form, with all short vowels. Everyday Palestinian verb. The imperative 'shut up' is iskut.
Active participle of sami3 'to hear'. It is used in phrases like 'saami3ak' (I hear you) and 'ma-ni saami3' (I can't hear).
Taa marbuta after م is e. The word is of MSA origin but very common in Palestinian speech and politics.
ح is 7, and the noun has a single syllable 7ajz. Used for booking a table, room or ticket.

meaning_fix: my brain has stopped working / my mind has gone blank (I can't think any more)
reasoning: مخ is mukhkh, 'my brain' is mukhkhi, and ق in wa'af is a glottal stop. It means my mind has gone blank or is too tired to think. 'Overwhelmed' is only part of that.
Taa marbuta after ر is a. Used for a bill or invoice, and also for a receipt.
Loanword with a long aa and a long oo, said diktaatoor. It is current in Palestinian conversation and news talk. The arabic script cannot show oo against uu.
From French bicyclette and used in Palestinian speech, alongside darraaja. I am unsure of the exact vowel pattern, whether baskleet or basikleet.
The initial hamza is a vowel seat, so the word is written isti3maar. MSA-origin political vocabulary that Palestinians use in conversation.
Literally 'my age is ... years'. Taa marbuta after ن is e. With the numbers 3 to 10 the plural sniin is used instead, as in '3umri khamas sniin'. The ellipsis is not romanized.
A Ramallah speaker says imta. The spelling with ي suggests the Syrian or Lebanese eemta, which Palestinians also understand. ى is the final a.
Of Egyptian origin but thoroughly used in Palestinian speech for 'never mind' and 'sorry'. The final vowel is a short i.
ق is a glottal stop in this everyday word, and ض is emphatic D. A judge is 'aaDi in conversation.
Loanword from English 'remote', said reemoot with long ee and oo. The usual everyday word for a TV remote.
The standard Palestinian 'where', with a long ee. It is one of the listed Palestinian markers, in place of MSA أين.
Urban Palestinian ث is t, so tlaate, with the first vowel dropped. Taa marbuta after ت is e. In a construction the number shortens to tlat.
il- assimilates to the sun letter س, giving is-salaame. Taa marbuta after م is e. Said by the person staying to the one leaving.
Urban ث is normally t in this word, so tabat rather than the MSA thabata. It means 'it stayed firm or was confirmed', and is somewhat more formal in register.
Formal or written word for round. In conversation a Ramallah speaker says mdawwar.
ma3 inno means 'even though' and bass means 'but'. The ellipsis is not romanized. Final bass is usually a little lengthened.

ظنّ is a doubled verb, so the first-person past is THanneet with the n doubled and the ending -eet. The verb is literary-leaning, and in everyday Palestinian speech fakkart inno is more usual. The realisation of ظ is the uncertain part.

meaning_fix: may God not disgrace you — said to a man as 'please' when asking a favour, or as a warm thank-you
reasoning: yihiin has a long ii, and -ak marks a male addressee. It is a politeness formula used both when requesting and when thanking, so 'polite request' covers only one of its uses.
